topic.subject: physics
topic.title: Energy stores, transfers and dissipation
topic.scopeBasis: TGS 2025-26 and 2026-27: energy stores and transfers
topic.overview: Energy is conserved but can move between stores by different pathways. Useful analysis identifies the initial and final stores and accounts for dissipated energy.
learningGoals: Recall the precise Year 8 scientific vocabulary and symbols.
Apply the idea to an unfamiliar example rather than relying on recognition.
Use the command word, show working where needed and include every mark point.
mustMemoriseRules: Energy stores include kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational potential, elastic potential, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear.
Energy is transferred mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed in a closed system; total energy is conserved.
Kinetic energy is associated with motion; gravitational potential energy with position in a gravitational field; elastic energy with deformation.
Chemical stores include fuels, foods and batteries.
Dissipation spreads energy into the thermal stores of the surroundings, making it less useful.
Friction and electrical resistance often cause heating.
A complete energy account names the initial store, transfer pathway and final stores without saying energy was used up.

mustMemoriseVocabulary.meaning: a way energy is held in a system
a process moving energy between stores
energy associated with particle motion and temperature
energy due to position in a gravitational field
energy associated with chemical bonds and reactions
spreading energy to surroundings, usually thermally
total energy remains constant in a closed system

workedExamples.prompt: Describe the energy changes as a ball falls.
workedExamples.answer: Energy transfers mechanically from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store; air resistance also increases thermal stores.
Energy transfers electrically from the battery's chemical store to light radiation and thermal stores of lamp and surroundings.

practicals.title: Energy transfers in a bouncing ball
practicals.aim: Observe useful and dissipative transfers during repeated bounces.
practicals.variables: IV: ball/material or drop height; DV: rebound height; controls: release method, surface and measurement method.
practicals.method: Drop without pushing from a measured height, video or measure successive rebound heights, repeat and compare ratios.
practicals.expectedResult: Rebound height falls because some energy is dissipated to thermal stores and sound on each impact.
practicals.safety: Keep the drop zone clear and use safe heights away from faces.
practicals.evaluation: Use slow-motion video, a fixed scale and repeated drops; discuss measurement parallax and air resistance.

commonMistakes: Saying energy is used up or disappears.
Calling light and sound stores rather than transfer pathways.
Listing stores without stating the transfer.
examTips: Use: from the ___ store, transferred by ___, to the ___ store(s).
Check that total input equals all outputs.
Call unwanted energy dissipated, not destroyed.
beforeStartingPractice: Read the key rules once, cover them, then retrieve them aloud or in writing.
Use MC first for confidence, but finish with typed, calculation, practical or explanation evidence.
After an error, study the explanation; the same concept returns later in a different format and again after 2 and 7 days.

practicals.title: Energy transfers in a bouncing ball
practicals.aim: Observe useful and dissipative transfers during repeated bounces.
practicals.variables: IV: ball/material or drop height; DV: rebound height; controls: release method, surface and measurement method.
practicals.method: Drop without pushing from a measured height, video or measure successive rebound heights, repeat and compare ratios.
practicals.expectedResult: Rebound height falls because some energy is dissipated to thermal stores and sound on each impact.
practicals.safety: Keep the drop zone clear and use safe heights away from faces.
practicals.evaluation: Use slow-motion video, a fixed scale and repeated drops; discuss measurement parallax and air resistance.
